536.t: Decline of studio orchestras and live music
536.s: Brown laments machines replacing live musicians, recalls studio orchestras under contract, and Quincy Jones's score-less film.
536.q: Yeah but let’s go back before that though. I mean when they first made movies they had a piano player playing in the pit. Only one piano player. And it went from that to orchestras, where there was an era for thirty, forty years where every major studio in Hollywood had a hundred and ten piece…

835.t: Changes in the studio scene and the musicians' union
835.s: Work has left Los Angeles for Canada and overseas for economic reasons; Humphrey says the union set useful scale but has not done enough for the production side.
835.q: Yeah. I mean again, technology and economics especially is changing lots of things. There’s less work, lots of musicians, so what happens is there’s an attrition rate and people fall by the wayside and it’s left with a certain core that pretty much doing all the work that’s remaining, at least in…

411.t: Teaching, CBS symphony and leaving studio work
411.s: Igoe built a teaching practice, earned more than playing, dropped off the studio call list, and notes musician residuals.
411.q: Well they had to cut down some men, yeah. I started teaching early in my career. I always liked to teach. And I have to say it myself because you don’t know but I’m good at it. I have the right disposition and the right patience and all that kind of stuff, and the right expertise. I’m very…

348.t: State of studio work, Local 47 and the contractors
348.s: The RMA, top contractors, and why calls have dried up, so he plays tributes to Goodman and Shaw.
348.q: There are still, let me say it this way. In the union there are about, I used to think there was 10,000 but I think it’s about half, it’s about 5,000 let’s say. Of that there’s a group called RMA, Recording Musician’s Association, which I am not a member of ‘cause I don’t do that much work anymore.…

499.s: Parker cringes at the loud, dated Simmons drum sound on the film Hoosiers.
499.q: Off hand, yeah. Not any movie that I was on. There’s some that I really — are hard to listen to now. There’s one called “Hoosiers” with Gene Hackman where they wanted me to play Simmons drums. And the producer and the director were really, really keen on the Simmons drum sound, all this electronic…

444.t: What a studio call involves; the Universal contractor Sandy DeCrescent
444.s: Shew explains doubles pay and mutes, and tells how a secretary became the Universal contractor.
444.q: A flugelhorn, not necessarily, or a piccolo trumpet, or anything they’re called doubles as you know, if the contractor calls you and says, “Bring a flugelhorn, they have to pay you for it whether you play it or not.” Okay? So if the call is out for the doubles, you know, when I was working at…

164.t: The 1950s as the best studio years, decline by the 1960s
164.s: The 50s studio work with Green, Steiner and the Newmans was lovely; by the early 60s eighth-triplet dates showed the decline.
164.q: Well Ozzie was in the 40s. In the 50s, the 50s actually were the best time as far as I’m concerned. I never came home complaining about the music on the date. I got to work with Johnny Green and Max Steiner and Alfred Newman, Lionel Newman, and the guys, you’d go in and there’d be a big beautiful…

823.t: Los Angeles studio TV work and its decline
823.s: Patrick Williams brought him into TV shows; he explains the union rule change, the 1990 decline and film contractors.
823.q: Different, but you see New York was already in a state of flux at that point. It was — studios were closing down left and right in favor of synthesizers, and everything was moving toward motion pictures and T.V. And Patrick Williams had called me up and said look, because I was looking for an…

85.t: Why film scoring changed and synthesizers
85.s: Carter blames changing tastes and self-contained groups for the end of the great film composers and says he used a synthesizer early.
85.q: Oh, I don’t know. I think it came about with the changes in the tastes of the young people. So many of the films were done with records, you know, a great deal of that, and small groups, as they called, self-contained groups, and they didn’t feel that they had the need for the Bernie Hermans…

86.t: Studio politics, his jazz reputation and the scene's decline
86.s: Edison says he got calls on reputation, that studio players envied jazz musicians, and that synthesizers ended the scene.
86.q: Oh definitely. There’s politics and politics. But I didn’t know that many people to be in politics. I didn’t know how to play no politics in the business. They either called me for what I could do or they didn’t call me at all. What little reputation that I had, it preceded me. They knew that I had…
